package_info.why_malicious: The package is explicitly crafted to execute a malicious payload immediately upon installation. It downloads an encrypted binary from a remote server, decrypts it using a byte-wise XOR operation, writes it to disk as a platform-specific executable (DLL for Windows, SO for Linux), executes the binary, and then erases evidence by deleting temporary files and replacing the malicious package.json with a clean version. The code is heavily obfuscated, adapts to the host OS, and is designed for stealth and persistence, indicating a targeted supply chain attack aimed at compromising developer environments for espionage or further lateral movement.

execution_context.file_location: package.json (postinstall script) and main JavaScript file (Windows-specific branch)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation (postinstall), the code checks if the operating system is Windows, downloads an encrypted payload from a remote server, decrypts it using a byte-wise XOR operation, writes the decrypted payload as a DLL file to disk, executes the DLL using rundll32, deletes the temporary DLL file, and replaces the malicious package.json with a clean version to erase evidence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code initiates a network request to download an encrypted binary during the postinstall phase, decrypts and executes it as a DLL, and then removes all traces by deleting files and restoring package.json. This sequence is highly indicative of a supply chain attack, as it enables remote code execution on developer machines without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not download, decrypt, and execute arbitrary DLLs during installation, nor do they attempt to erase evidence by modifying package.json or deleting temporary files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may download platform-specific binaries for native modules, but they do not execute arbitrary DLLs with rundll32, nor do they perform anti-forensic actions such as cleaning up package.json to hide their activity.
key_indicators: postinstall script that triggers network download and execution of a DLL
byte-wise XOR decryption of downloaded payload
use of rundll32 to execute a dynamically written DLL
immediate deletion of the DLL after execution
replacement of package.json to remove evidence of the malicious script

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation (postinstall), if the operating system is Linux, the code downloads an encrypted payload from a remote server, decrypts it using a byte-wise XOR operation, writes the decrypted payload as a shared object (.so) file to disk, makes it executable, executes the .so file, deletes the temporary file, and replaces the malicious package.json with a clean version to erase evidence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code adapts to the host OS, downloads and decrypts a remote binary, executes it as a shared object, and then erases evidence by deleting files and restoring package.json. This behavior is characteristic of advanced malware designed for stealthy compromise of developer systems.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not execute arbitrary binaries from remote sources during installation, nor do they attempt to hide their actions by cleaning up package.json or deleting evidence immediately after execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some build tools may download prebuilt binaries for native modules, but they do not execute them as standalone processes or perform anti-forensic cleanup of package.json.
key_indicators: OS detection and branching for Linux-specific payload delivery
network download and execution of a .so file during postinstall
byte-wise XOR decryption of the payload
immediate deletion of the .so file after execution
replacement of package.json to remove evidence of the malicious script

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering the postinstall script defined in package.json.
The script checks the operating system and downloads the corresponding encrypted payload (DLL for Windows, SO for Linux) from a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload decryption and preparation for execution

attack_chain.action: The downloaded payload is decrypted using a byte-wise XOR operation and written to disk as a temporary DLL or SO file.
The malicious binary is executed (rundll32 for Windows, chmod +x and direct execution for Linux).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code runs on the victim system

attack_chain.action: Temporary files (DLL/SO) are deleted and the malicious package.json is replaced with a clean version to erase evidence of compromise.

behavioral_signatures: postinstall script that downloads and executes remote binaries during npm package installation
byte-wise XOR decryption routines applied to downloaded payloads
OS-specific branching logic for payload delivery and execution
immediate deletion of temporary DLL or SO files after execution
modification or replacement of package.json post-install to remove evidence
file_indicators: creation and rapid deletion of temporary DLL files (e.g., temp.dll) on Windows during npm install
creation and rapid deletion of temporary SO files (e.g., temp.so) on Linux during npm install
package.json file being replaced or modified immediately after installation
presence of obfuscated JavaScript code in the main entry point
network_indicators: outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to suspicious or untrusted domains (e.g., https://malicious-domain.com/payload, https://malicious-domain.com/payload-linux) during npm install
downloads of binary payloads from remote servers during the postinstall phase
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for postinstall scripts that initiate outbound network requests, especially those that download and execute binaries. Flag packages that modify or replace package.json after installation, or that create and quickly delete DLL/SO files. Detect the presence of byte-wise XOR decryption routines and OS-specific branching logic in installation scripts. Correlate these behaviors with outbound connections to untrusted domains during install time to identify potential supply chain attacks.
